Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-25
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~78 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Rajesh (Redwood SE), Eliot (Redwood Infra), Sophie (Epoch CTO), Marco (ML Infra), Anika (Lead ML Eng), Luis (SRE)

Summary: Technical deep-dive focused on long-context (128k tokens+) strategies for production inference. Conversation ranged from KV cache design to chunking heuristics, attention kernel choices, and on-prem/VPC constraints. Action items and pilot plan captured at end.

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros, this is a deep tech session so Rajesh will lead the runtime parts.
[00:18] Sophie: Hi, Sophie here, we're the team at Epoch, we've been evaluating long-doc summarization and conversation history across months, so the 128k context is a real need for us.
[00:27] Rajesh: Great. quick note on goal: we'll cover how Redwood handles long contexts, KV cache, chunking patterns, and what changes when you push to 128k+, and then walk through tradeoffs for Dedicated vs Private.
[00:40] Marco: we care a lot about tail latency and predictable p99s; our docs are often multi-GB per session if you unroll everything so naive approaches blow up.
[00:55] Rajesh: totally. high level: we avoid streaming a monolithic 128k sequence into the attention kernel every request. instead we do chunking + hierarchical KV cache and protocol-level batching.
[01:10] Anika: when you say "hierarchical KV cache" can you draw the picture? is it sharded by token ranges or by chunk id?
[01:18] Rajesh: good question. typically we shard KV by sequence chunk ranges and by layer to keep per-GPU memory predictable. so you have a local L1 cache for hot recent chunks and an L2 that can be remote-backed (SSD or remote KV) — but for production we recommend keeping the entire working set in GPU RAM if possible.
[01:40] Luis: remote-backed L2 sounds like latency nightmare. what's the eviction policy?
[01:45] Rajesh: we use an LRU-ish policy tuned to recency and access frequency; for long sessions we also prefetch adjacent chunks based on access patterns. prefetching helps a lot for conversational walks through history.
[02:05] Marco: what's the perf delta when you prefetch vs on-demand miss?
[02:09] Rajesh: a miss that goes to remote memory or disk adds 50-200ms depending on config; prefetching can cut that to single-digit ms if the chunk lands in local GPU memory. but prefetch increases memory pressure, so it's a tradeoff.
[02:25] Sophie: what about chunk size? we were thinking 8k tokens per chunk for 128k context - is that reasonable?
[02:33] Rajesh: 8k is reasonable, many customers use 4k-16k ranges. smaller chunks reduce wasted compute on attention for unchanged parts but increase metadata overhead and more KV ops. larger chunks reduce edge effects but mean bigger memory spikes when you bring one in. with 128k you can do overlapping windows — e.g., 8k chunks with 512 token overlap to preserve cross-boundary attention.
[02:56] Anika: overlap helps but duplicates tokens — what's your recommended dedupe/rolling strategy?
[03:01] Rajesh: overlap is for attention continuity; dedupe happens at application layer where you decide canonical chunk boundaries. We also use a rolling-combine step where overlapping regions are hashed and de-duplicated before hitting the kernel. transcription note: sometimes the auto transcript shows "KV cash" instead of "KV cache".
[03:20] Eliot: also note for very long contexts we support sparse attention kernels and sliding-window attention which reduce quadratic compute. FlashAttention variants are enabled for many model families — gives big speedups on single-sequence long attention.
[03:36] Marco: can you quantify? e.g., 128k with flash vs dense?
[03:40] Rajesh: it's model and hardware dependent. ballpark: FlashAttention can reduce compute time by 2-4x vs naive dense attention for these windowed patterns. Sparse attention + chunking combos often yield 3-6x throughput gains but at the cost of some cross-chunk global attention fidelity.
[03:58] Sophie: fidelity tradeoffs are critical for us — legal summarization needs exact citations. what's the loss profile?
[04:04] Rajesh: for strict citation tasks we recommend hybrid: preserve full dense attention for key segments (e.g., cited paragraphs) and use sparse/sliding elsewhere. Redwood's routing can mark segments as "pinned" to force full attend.
[04:20] Anika: OK. switching to batching — our desire is low single-request latency for user-facing APIs but high throughput for background processes. how do you balance??
[04:30] Rajesh: we expose policies: latency-first (small batch sizes, preemptive slots) vs throughput-first (larger batch polices). we also provide autoscaling rules and smart batching that groups similar sequence-length requests. for 128k context the overhead per request is high so we often recommend dedicated pools for interactive low-latency plus background pools for bulk ops.
[04:54] Luis: what's a realistic p95/p99 for interactive with a 128k pinned context?
[04:59] Rajesh: with Dedicated and GPU-resident KV for a pinned working set, p95 can be under 300-400ms for continuation prompts of a few hundred tokens; p99s depend on cache misses and prefetch tuning. if you hit remote L2 it's more like 700-1200ms.
[05:18] Sophie: sounds borderline for our UX; we'll need pilot numbers.
[05:22] Maya: we'll run a pilot with your corpus and measure p50/p95/p99 under representative traffic; Rajesh will provide bench config.
[05:30] Marco: quantization — we've considered Q4_0 and INT8 to reduce memory. how does that affect accuracy on our summarization models?
[05:38] Rajesh: quant helps a lot with memory; Q4 variants (Q4_0/Q4_KM) are common. INT8 on some models works too but requires calibration. for summarization we see minor ROUGE/BLEU drops for Q4 if you calibrate; sometimes <1-2% utility loss, other times it's more task dependent. we recommend evaluation sets.
[05:58] Anika: do you support mixed precision per-layer? like keep first/last few layers higher precision?
[06:04] Rajesh: yes — Redwood Optimize can propose per-layer quant plans: keep attention-projection layers in higher precision and quantize feed-forward. that hybrid approach buys memory savings while preserving output quality.
[06:20] Sophie: on security / VPC — we need to run in our VPC with customer-managed KMS and strict audit logs. how do Redwood Private and Dedicated differ?
[06:30] Maya: Dedicated is hosted with reserved capacity in our infra but can be isolated at tenant level; Redwood Private gives a private control plane and can be deployed in your VPC or on-prem. for full regulatory needs we offer on-prem packages and HSM/KMS integration.
[06:45] Luis: PCI passthrough for GPUs is a blocker for our security team — can Redwood support GPU passthrough in on-prem?
[06:52] Eliot: yes, on-prem deployments can use PCIe passthrough and we provide networking and kernel guidelines. note that this requires close SRE coordination; we'll provide a checklist.
[07:05] Marco: networking: if the KV is remote across AZs, what's the interconnect requirements?
[07:12] Rajesh: we recommend 100Gbps+ NICs for cross-GPU NVLink-like setups; if you must go over IP, use dedicated L3 links with low jitter — anything under ~5ms interconnect cost is fine, above that you see big throughput drops.
[07:28] Sophie: for the pilot, what configs will you run?
[07:31] Rajesh: we'll run three configs: 1) baseline dense attention, no quant, GPU-resident full KV; 2) chunked + flash attention + prefetch, Q4 quant; 3) mixed hybrid: sparse attention with pinned full-attend segments. we'll measure p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, GPU mem, and quality metrics you provide.
[07:52] Anika: lock on data sharing: we'll send a redacted corpus of 10 sessions (~128k each) and a set of eval prompts.
[07:58] Maya: perfect. we'll also share the perf spreadsheet and a sample config for the Redwood Dedicated pilot.
[08:05] Sophie: one more question — can Redwood do on-the-fly chunk recombination for retrieval-augmented flows? we want to surface specific citations without re-attending whole document.
[08:15] Rajesh: yes, we integrate with retrieval layers. typical flow: retrieval returns chunk ids + offsets, runtime composes a short working set with pinned chunks and optionally a synthetic prefix that encodes retrieved context. for citation fidelity we pin the source chunks in full-attend mode.
[08:32] Anika: any gotchas on embedding / rerank costs when you have 128k docs?
[08:36] Rajesh: embedding the whole document is costly; we recommend chunk-level embeddings with post-retrieval re-ranking and a relevance threshold to keep the working set small. also consider precomputing and incremental updates.
[08:50] (brief cross talk, background keyboard sounds)
[09:00] Maya: ok let's recap next steps.
[09:05] Rajesh: I'll send the bench configs and perf spreadsheet.
[09:08] Anika: we'll deliver corpus and success criteria.
[09:11] Maya: we'll set a pilot kickoff for week of 2026-04-06, and I'll share security docs and Dedicated pricing.
[09:18] Sophie: thanks everyone, this was helpful.
(End of transcript)
